en: Preface to the Comprehensive Survey of Bestowing Food by Zishī:
To examine this in detail, there are three kinds of giving (*dāna*): first, the gift of material wealth; second, the gift of the Dharma; and third, the gift of fearlessness.
Now, can the gift of the food of the Dharma not encompass all three types of giving? It is because it uses food and drink to provide relief to others.

First, the hunger and emptiness [of the recipients] are one and the same. Second, the application of the *dhāraṇī*-food method ensures that as the food enters their mouths, it accords with the Dharma.
Third, once the Dharma-food has been bestowed, it causes all their terrors to be entirely abandoned and them to be liberated from the dark realms of existence.

Not only does this apply to what is bestowed, but for the bestower as well, the five fruits are immediately attained and the two adornments shall be fully prepared; thus, the bestowal of Dharma-food also encompasses both.

Is it not the case that both self-benefit and benefit for others are contained therein? That which is extolled by all Buddhas and praised by the multitude of sages is certainly beyond the reach of conjecture or debate.
Yet, those who fail to discern this often say: "I am devoted to the fundamental and do not pursue the derivative.
But what indeed is the purpose of those who devote their will to bestowing blessings? Alas! Among the myriad practices, there is Prajñā.
When one acts as a guide, the three spheres (trimaṇḍala) are empty and still; even if one were to practice giving throughout the entire day, what harm could there be?
If, however, one merely clings to literalism and falls into the view of nihilism, one will deviate from the Way by a great distance.

*Shishi tonglan* (A Comprehensive Survey of Food Offerings) was compiled by the Dharma Master Xiaokong, who was known as Shi Zhi. It appears that the Master, having previously mastered the methods for offering food, found them to be simple yet effective and concise.
Success lies in gathering those scriptural texts that pertain to this subject and compiling them into this book, so that everyone may clearly understand their origins;
would not the benevolence of the Duke’s kindness toward all things then be vast indeed? I was fortunate enough to obtain this book in the capital;
upon casting my eyes over it once, I could not help but marvel at its excellence, and have thus selected several copies to collate and verify its characters.
That this work was carved in wood and published as both a harmonious instruction and a guide is intended so that the method of bestowing food may overflow inexhaustibly.

The purpose for compiling this book truly lies herein. If those who read it well believe in it with firm conviction and practice it with sincere integrity, then the three kinds of giving can be accomplished, the five fruits can be attained, and the two adornments can be perfected—thus not failing the Master Xiaogong.
This is what I have long hoped for.
Written on a clear morning in the middle month of autumn in the fourth year of the Genroku era, the year of Xinwei.
Recorded respectfully by the śramaṇa Jiānshān of Ānyáng Lǜsì on the eastern shore of the lake.

The benefit of this gift of the Dharma-food is vast indeed! It not only causes others to escape the dark paths and be reborn in the good realms, so that they may take refuge in the Triple Gem and achieve perfect enlightenment, but it also enables people to, in the near term, manifest the five fruits, and in the distant term, accomplish the two adornments.
It is truly the essential ford for the mutual salvation of self and others, and the wondrous path for entering the supreme stage of the Buddhas. I have humbly...

I have observed that throughout distant lands and nearby regions, whether among the ordained or the laity, there are many who follow this practice; yet, those who are ignorant of its underlying principles are likewise numerous.

Consequently, in the course of perusing the scriptural teachings, I have transcribed every passage related to the offering of food (śrāddha), gathering them together in great abundance until I was unaware of their volume.
On days of leisure, I arranged them into a single volume, and thus titled it: [The Ritual Manual for the Offering of Food].

Thus it is said: "This 'Comprehensive Survey of Bestowing Food' is now completed. Hereafter, may those who encounter this writing give rise to the mind of compassion and wisdom, and further broaden their practice of formless giving. So it is said.

At that time, the World-Honored One was at the Nyagrodha Monastery in the city of Kapilavastu,
surrounded on all sides by bhikṣus, bodhisattvas, and countless sentient beings, as he preached the Dharma to them. At that moment, Ānanda,
dwelling alone in a pure place with his mind focused in single-minded concentration, saw a hungry ghost after the third watch of that night.
A hungry ghost named Mianran stood before Ānanda and said to him, "In three days from now, your life will come to an end, and you shall immediately be reborn among these hungry ghosts.

When Ānanda heard these words, his heart was filled with terror, and he asked the hungry ghost, "What plan can I devise to escape this calamity and avoid such suffering? At that time, the hungry ghost—
The ghost replied to Ānanda: "If you, at dawn, can provide alms of one *droṇa* of food and drink— measured by the Magadhan *droṇa*—
to a hundred thousand *nayuta* of *gangesu-vālukopama* hungry ghosts, as well as to a hundred thousand Brahmins and sages,
and furthermore make offerings to the Triple Gem on my behalf, you shall gain an increase in your lifespan and cause me to [attain liberation]."
Having escaped the suffering of the hungry ghosts (preta), they were reborn in the heavens; Ānanda saw them with their faces aflame.

Yet the bodies of these hungry ghosts were emaciated, withered, and extremely hideous; fire blazed from their faces, their throats were like needles, their hair was disheveled, and their fur and claws were long and sharp.
Their bodies appeared as if burdened by a heavy load, and hearing such discordant words, they were struck with great terror, the hairs on their bodies standing on end.
They all immediately rose from their seats and hurried to where the Buddha was. Prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, they bowed at the Buddha’s feet;
trembling in both body and mind, they addressed the Buddha, saying: "Save us, World-Honored One! Save us, Sugata! In three days our lives will come to an end.
Last night we saw a face of a hungry ghost who spoke to us, saying: 'In three days you shall surely...'"
When my life was ending, I was born among the hungry ghosts (preta). I immediately asked them, "By what means or stratagem may I escape this suffering?

The hungry ghosts replied, "If you can provide food and drink for hundreds of thousands of nayutas of hungry ghosts as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as for hundreds of thousands of brahmins and various sages, you shall increase your lifespan, World-Honored One. How may we now obtain [this]?"
To free them from this suffering, at that time the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "Do not fear now;
there is a different expedient means by which you may cause such hungry ghosts, brahmins, sages, and others to receive food. Do not give rise to sorrow or distress. The Buddha said:
"Ānanda, there is a dhāraṇī called 'Light of All Virtues' (Sarvaguṇaprabhāsa) of immeasurable power. If anyone recites it..."

This dhāraṇī constitutes the act of having already bestowed food and drink—measuring four *droṇas* and nine *āḍhakas* of Magadha—before each of hundreds of thousands of *koṭis*, *nayutas*, and *śatasahasras* of *pretas* as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as sixty-eight *koṭis*, *nayutas*, and *śatasahasras* of Brahmins and various sages. The Buddha told Ānanda: "In the past, I..."
In the past, when I was a brahmin, I received this dhāraṇī from Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and the Tathāgata Lokeśvaraguṇabala.

By means of this dhāraṇī, I shall be able to provide food in full measure to immeasurable and incalculable hungry ghosts, brahmins, sages, and others through the skillful means of my giving. By my giving to all these...
Because the hungry ghosts have consumed it, they shall abandon this body and attain rebirth in the heavens.
Ānanda, you should now receive and uphold this dhāraṇī to protect yourself. Then he spoke the mantra: [Mantra follows]
Then, recite: *Sarvathāgata-vajrodake Oṃ Vāra Svara Hūṃ*. The Buddha said:
"Ānanda, if one wishes to perform this rite of offering food, first take rice and other foods and place them upon a clean plate."
Recite this dhāraṇī mantra over the food seven times within a vessel. Standing inside the doorway with arms extended, place the dish outside on clean ground and snap your fingers seven times.

Having performed this offering, there will be hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of hungry ghosts, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and before each and every one of those hungry ghosts, there will be a māgha [of food].
Four *dōu* and nine *dōu* of food and drink [suffice] for these ghosts and others, so that they are all completely satiated.
Once these hungry ghosts have eaten this food, they all abandon their ghostly bodies and are reborn entirely in the heavens.
Furthermore, Ānanda, if bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās can constantly recite this dhāraṇī and offer food and drink, [the same result shall follow].
They shall immediately become endowed with immeasurable merit and their lives shall be prolonged; they shall achieve the merit of making offerings to hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Tathāgatas;
their complexion shall be fresh and pure, and their majestic virtue and memory shall be powerful.

All non-humans, such as the Bhūtas, Pretas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and various hungry ghosts, shall all stand in awe of this person, unable to bear looking upon them. This person shall immediately [attain... for them.
Having achieved and perfected great power and diligent exertion, he spoke again:
"Ānanda, if you wish to give food to brahmins and sages, you should take food and drink, fill a bowl with it, and recite this dhāraṇī mantra over the food seven times.
Then, pour it into flowing water as a complete offering to immeasurable koṭis of hundreds of thousands of Ganges-sands of brahmins."
The gatekeepers, the various sages, and others partook of the celestial food.
Once those brahmins and sages had eaten this meal, their faculties became complete and perfect, and they were endowed with auspiciousness. Each made his own aspiration and praised the donor;
the mind of the person who gave the food became purified, and he swiftly realized the majestic power of Brahmā, constantly practicing pure conduct until its full perfection.
The merit of making offerings to as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Ganges Rivers ensures that one will always prevail over all enemies.
If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās wish to make offerings to the Triple Gem,
they should prepare incense, flowers, food, and drink, and recite this dhāraṇī mantra while consecrating the offerings.

By making offerings of food, incense, flowers, and so forth twenty-one times to the Triple Gem, these sons and daughters of good family will fully accomplish the wondrous offerings of the devas as well as the unsurpassed offerings;
they shall be honored and praised by all Tathāgatas, and their lands, the Triple Gem, and the Buddhas shall be remembered, extolled, and lauded by the devas who protect them. The Buddha said to you:
Ānanda, you should protect yourself and also extensively explain this for the sake of all sentient beings,
so that all sentient beings may achieve and be fully endowed with immeasurable merit, and in every lifetime they are born into, they shall always encounter hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddhas.
The *Buddhabhāṣita-mukha-dahana-preta-tāraṇī-dhāraṇī-mantra-sūtra* concludes here.

According to the *Shishi xuzhi* (Essentials for Bestowing Food) and the Shu edition of the *Yogatantra-guhyamantra*, there is a "Nectar Water Mantra" (*amṛtodaka-mantra*) said to have been translated by Śikṣānanda and to appear after the *Mukhadahana-sūtra*. However, upon examining the Tripitaka editions, this is not recorded; it has likely been omitted during subsequent transcription and carving.

Now, I have respectfully transcribed it from the *Guhyamantra* collection and appended it to the end of this sūtra, hoping to supplement its deficiencies. Furthermore, that [text] also contains the "Milk Ocean Mantra," the "Single-Syllable Water Wheel Mantra," along with verses and so forth, all of which shall likewise be transmitted. Or perhaps... [there may be].
What is employed here is not without its basis in scriptural authority).

A single drop of the inconceivable Dharma of ambrosia, Pervading with refreshing coolness—
this was all spoken by the Buddha Vairocanagarbha as the *Dhāraṇī for Bestowing the Ocean of Milk*.
*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ baṃ* (as transcribed in the Taishō Tripiṭaka, following the phonetic glosses).

Next, for the sake of all sentient beings, whether hidden or manifest, entering the Vairocana Tathāgata’s Single-Syllable Water-Wheel Contemplation so that all beings may freely drink ten *hu* of the Dharma-water of ambrosia, the dhāraṇī is as follows:
Oṃ baṃ baṃ baṃ baṃ. This is the Vairocana teaching, the gateway to liberation through nectar.
By the empowerment of these great secret words, may the food of dharma-joy and the food of meditative bliss pervade the entire dharmadhātu;
may all the hosts of spirits and deities obtain the flavor of sudhā.
Forever eliminating the perceptions of hunger and thirst, one immediately realizes the stage of non-birth.
The Tathāgata Amṛtarāja praises the son of the unconditioned, Yang Jie.
It is said that the various devas cast famous medicinal herbs into the great ocean and, by rubbing them against the mountain of wondrous jewels, they produced the flavor of ambrosia.

Those who taste it prolong their lifespans without premature death or calamity; the Tathāgata bestows this Dharma-food, filling the great trichiliocosm, so that all who suffer from craving may forever sever the root of birth and death.
I bow my head to the King of Nectar, whose single meal pervades all things.

There are matters that are simple yet easy to follow; there are things that are minute yet provide great salvation; there are efficacies that are manifold and whose response is swift.
These three [benefits] are fully contained within this sutra. Furthermore, when setting forth a single vessel of food, one recites the mantra seven times while snapping the fingers to bestow it;

the mantra itself consists of no more than a few phrases—this is its ease of practice. It reaches down to the bottomless springs and encompasses the nine realms, such that even the *yánkǒu* (flaming-mouth) ghosts, whose number is as incalculable as dust motes in the sands, all find sweet satisfaction and their bellies are filled—this is its great salvation. As for the matter of karmic retribution:

This principle universally encompasses the three periods of time; those whose karma is vast and profound are said to experience its fruition in the present life, such as the prolongation of one’s lifespan—this is what is meant by a swift summons [of retribution].
The regulations of the Dharma King are straightforward and clear, ready to be put into practice.
Now, a single morsel of food or a single ladle of water has utility that is inexhaustible; yet those who hear this cannot help but be perplexed. If one were merely to infer...

The efficacy of divine mantras returns to an unfathomable principle; how, then, can one be confused? A dragon is but a single-scaled creature, yet when it obtains water from a puddle at a horse’s hoofprint, it disperses it through the six voids to become a vast flood.
How much more so for the divine mantra of the Most Holy and Most Benevolent One, which exhausts the ultimate transformations of the entire Dharma-realm!
To have a parched belly and a parched mouth, sinking into the darkness for kalpas on end, looking up to heaven with no one to whom to appeal—is this not a situation where only compassion can save?
For one whose heart is filled with compassionate empathy, even a single act of kindness performed by extending an arm—such as providing a single meal—is surely possible.
How magnificent! This is truly what is meant by "broadly bestowing benefits to relieve the multitude. Why must it be said that even Yao and Shun found this difficult?

Furthermore, if one can extend forgiveness for one's own hunger and thirst to the hunger and thirst of others, then even if it involves labor, it is still feasible; how much more so when the method is simple and easy to follow! As the Sūtra says: "It is like making an offering..."
The phrase "hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddhas" not only reveals the greatness of their merit, but also serves as a warning to exercise caution before bestowing [gifts].
One must certainly act with a sincere heart; doing so will immediately bring forth the five fruits. These five fruits are: first, longevity; second, physical beauty;
third, strength; fourth, eloquence; and fifth, peace. These are clearly stated in the texts, so there is no need for further elaboration. Truly, one [act of faith]...

When the seeds of merit are sown there, the five blessings flourish here; it is like the relationship between a shadow and its echo. How could there be anyone who hears of such diligent goodness and yet does not transform themselves?
This scripture has been translated twice; this version consists of eighty-three lines with one character per line, totaling one thousand four hundred and thirteen words.
It is the translation by the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra, though it merely adds the [sections on] the four Tathāgatas and the four...

Regarding those who employ mantras for specific purposes, they may choose to retain or omit them at will; since official duties and worldly affairs leave no leisure for extensive practice, it is sufficient in principle to simply recite the single mantra for transforming food.
In the version translated by Atiśa, there is only this one mantra, as the ritual requirements for the *piṇḍapātra* (food offering) are fully contained therein;
thus, I shall not trouble you with further elaboration.

At that time, the World-Honored One was at the Nyagrodha Monastery in the city of Kapilavastu, together with various bhikṣus...
The Buddha was surrounded before and behind by an assembly of countless bodhisattvas as he preached the Dharma.

At that time, Ānanda was dwelling alone in a quiet place, reflecting upon the teachings he had received. Then, after the third watch of the night had passed, he saw a hungry ghost named Yāmukha (Flaming Mouth).
Its form was hideous, its body withered and emaciated, fire blazed from its mouth, and its throat was like a needle.
With hair bristling and disheveled, and claws and fangs long and sharp—most terrifying—he stood before Ānanda and said to him:
"In three days from now, your life will come to an end, and you shall be reborn among these hungry ghosts.
Having heard these words, Ānanda’s heart was filled with fear and dread, and he asked the hungry ghost: "If after my death I am reborn as a hungry ghost, what should I do?"
"What expedient means can be used to escape this suffering? At that time, the hungry ghost said to Ānanda:

"If tomorrow you can practice giving by bestowing food and drink—one *droṇa* each, using the measures employed in the kingdom of Magadha—to one hundred thousand *nayuta* of hungry ghosts as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, as well as to one hundred thousand Brahmin seers and others, and furthermore..."
"I have made offerings to the Triple Gem so that you may increase your lifespan, and that I may be freed from the suffering of the hungry ghosts and be reborn in the heavens.
Ānanda saw this hungry ghost with a body emaciated, withered, and extremely hideous;
fire blazed from its mouth, its throat was as narrow as the point of a needle, its hair was disheveled, and its claws and fangs were long and sharp. Furthermore, he heard such discordant [cries].

Upon hearing these words, he was struck with great terror; his hair stood on end, and he immediately rose from his seat, hastened to where the Buddha was, and prostrated himself before the Buddha’s feet.
With his body trembling, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "I pray that you will save me from this suffering. Why is this?
While I was dwelling in a quiet place, reflecting upon the Dharma I had received, I saw a *yāmuka* hungry ghost who spoke to me, saying: 'You have transgressed...'"
"In three days your life will surely come to an end, and you shall be reborn among the hungry ghosts. I then asked, "How may I escape this suffering?

The hungry ghost replied, "If you can now provide various kinds of food and drink for hundreds of thousands of nayutas of hungry ghosts as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as for hundreds of thousands of brahmins and rishis, you shall increase your lifespan and remain in the world."
"Venerable One, how can I now prepare food for so many hungry ghosts, rishis, and others? At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:

"Do not be afraid now! I have a skillful means by which you will be able to provide various foods and drinks for hundreds of thousands of *gaṅgā*-sands of hungry ghosts, as well as for the various brahmins and rishis. Do not give rise to grief or distress."
He addressed Ānanda: "There is a dhāraṇī named 'Infinite Majestic Virtue, Sovereign Radiance, and Supreme Wondrous Power.

If there are those who recite this dhāraṇī, they will be able to provide sufficient and exquisite food and drink for koṭis, nayutas, hundreds of thousands, and as many as the sands of the Ganges of hungry ghosts, Brahmins, sages, and others; such multitudes as these..."
Each and every one of them obtained a *māgadha* measure used in the kingdom of Magadha; seven times seven measures of food were given to Ānanda.

Because I, in a previous life, was a Brahmin who received this *vidyā-dhāraṇī* from Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja, I was able to scatter and bestow it upon immeasurable hungry ghosts and various sages.
By means of various kinds of food and drink such as these, all hungry ghosts shall be liberated from their bodies of suffering and attain rebirth in the heavens.
Ānanda, you should now receive and uphold this; your merit and lifespan will both increase. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke a dhāraṇī for Ānanda, saying:
*Namo sarvatathāgate vairocanate oṃ sara sara hūṃ.* The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"If there are sons or daughters of good family who wish to seek long life, merit, and increasing prosperity..."
One will swiftly be able to fulfill the *dānapāramitā*. At dawn and at all times, without any hindrance, take a clean vessel and fill it with pure water;
place a small amount of parched grain flour, cakes, rice, and other foods within it.
Press the vessel with your right hand and recite the aforementioned *dhāraṇī* seven times. Then, while holding [the vessel], recite the names of the four Tathāgatas.
Homage to the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna. Namo bhagavate prabuddharatnāya tathāgatāya. (1) (2)
By the power of reciting the name of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, one is able to destroy all ghosts;
the evil karma and karmic obstructions of stinginess accumulated over many lifetimes are extinguished, and one immediately attains the perfection of merit and virtue.
Homage to the Tathāgata Subhavarṇa. Namo bhagavate surūpāya tathāgatāya.
By the power of reciting the name of the Tathāgata Subhakāya, one is able to destroy the hideous and evil forms of all ghosts and immediately attain a body endowed with perfect physical marks.
Homage to the Tathāgata Vipulaśarīra.
Namo bhagavate vipulagātrāya tathāgatāya. (2) By virtue of reciting the name of the Tathāgata Vipulagātra and through his empowerment,
the throats of all hungry ghosts are made wide and spacious.
May the food offered satisfy you to your heart's content.
Namo virabhayavigatabhayāya tathāgatāya. Namo vāgīśvarāya āvartakārāya tathāgatāya.
Gatāya: By virtue of reciting the name of the Tathāgata Vītabhaya and through his empowerment, all terrors of the hungry ghosts are completely extinguished,
and they are freed from the realm of pretas.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "If sons of noble family and others, having invoked the names of the four Tathāgatas for empowerment, snap their fingers seven times and take a food vessel, extend their arms over clean ground and pour out the contents;

having performed this offering, there will appear before them in the four directions hundreds of thousands of nayutas of hungry ghosts as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each with a māṇava [attendant]."
Having received these offerings of seventy-seven *hu* of food from the kingdom of Ta, all these hungry ghosts were completely satisfied;

they all cast off their ghostly bodies and were reborn in the heavens. Ānanda, if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who constantly empower food and drink with this mantra and the names of the four Tathāgatas to give as alms to hungry ghosts...

Because it illuminates all darkness and brings about the perfection of *prajñā*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "That which is equal regarding food is also equal regarding the Dharma.

Therefore, the power of a single mantra can encompass all others without depending on their multitude.
Furthermore, there are the *Amṛta Sūtra* and a small scroll, both of which have lost translations and are not to be used. Next, to correctly demonstrate the method, the Sūtra says:

"If one wishes to perform this rite of offering food (*bali*), first take a clean vessel, fill it with pure water, and place within it a small amount of food and drink, as well as various [other offerings]."
Press the vessel of cakes and rice with the right hand and recite the mantra seven times, and so forth.

When the recitation is finished, snap the fingers seven times and extend the arms to pour the food vessel onto the clean ground (the method concludes here; Śikṣānanda’s translation states "standing inside the gate, extending the arms outside the door, place the dish on the clean ground," and does not mention "pouring").
Having performed this offering, in the four directions there are hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Before each of the hungry ghosts, there appeared seven times seven *droṇas* of food from the kingdom of Magadha;
having received this food, they were all completely satiated. All these hungry ghosts cast off their ghostly bodies and were reborn in the heavens.

Regarding the bestowal upon the Brahmin seers and the making of offerings to the Triple Gem, one may readily see this in the sutras. (When reciting the mantra, further add visualization: since it is already most excellent, visualize the color of the food and drink within the vessel...)

Its flavor is inexhaustible and its universal bestowal is never depleted; it is like the single bowl of fragrant rice in the room of Vimalakīrti that sufficed for the entire assembly without any lack, and like the small amount of rice from Cunda that filled the great multitude at the Twin Śāla Trees—neither too much nor too little.

To have faith in this *dhāraṇī* is inconceivable; the food, color, and fragrance are inconceivable, and the minds of sentient beings are also inconceivable. Why, then, should one be deluded? Third, the exhortation to practice: This sutra is the true art of longevity.
Venerable Ānanda extended his life by three days, fulfilling his hundred-year lifespan when he was certain to die.

Venerable Sir, when the five fruits [of health]—form, strength, eloquence, tranquility, and longevity—are fully attained, and the two adornments [of merit and wisdom] are properly prepared, this truly depends upon the giving of even a single morsel of food.

As the Sūtra says: "If one constantly empowers food and drink with this mantra and gives it to the hungry ghosts, it is equal in merit to making offerings to hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Tathāgatas, without any difference."

Furthermore, one’s lifespan is extended (longevity), one’s complexion is bright and pure (form), one is endowed with great strength (power), and one possesses majestic virtue and a powerful memory (eloquence).
No non-humans, yakṣas, or rākṣasas dare to harm them (peace). Moreover, they can accomplish immeasurable merit and a long life (the two adornments). [Note:

Since the previous five fruits already include longevity and principle, there is logically no need for these to appear again; we know with certainty that in this context, wisdom constitutes "life," while the five fruits and the two adornments are clearly manifest in the text.]

How great this is! To be able to perform such vast Buddha-work in a mere moment; to be able to turn a morsel of food into a great assembly of offerings, constantly being reborn in the Brahma heavens and even attaining Buddhahood—if this is so for a single day, how much more so for a month, how much more so for a year, and how much more so for an entire lifetime?
What wise person, having heard this, would not believe it, and having believed it, would not put it into practice?
The ritual text for offering food is the same as before:
place the food and drink in a copper vessel and sprinkle it with pure water.

Facing the vessel while standing, arouse a mind of compassion, recite the names of the Triple Gem (three times), and the Greatly Compassionate Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva (three times to break the obstacles of the hungry ghosts). Having finished the recitation:
Holding the food with the left hand and pressing down on the vessel with the right index finger, focus the mind and fix the eyes upon it while reciting the *dhāraṇī* seven times.
When the recitation is finished, snap the fingers seven times; then, extending the hands downward, perform the *abhaya-dāna* (gift of fearlessness) for a long moment.
Immediately thereafter, pour out the food and place it upon clean ground. Joining the palms, offer this prayer: "I, the śramaṇa [Name], now..."
Recite the *Aparimitāyur-jñāna-vighnāntaka-tejorāja-prabhāsa-suvikrāntabala-dhāraṇī* to empower the food and drink,
which you universally bestow upon the assembly of hungry ghosts. May the Great Powerful Noble Being, King Yama, whose heart is perfumed with compassion,
universally gather the assembly of hungry ghosts as numerous as the sands of immeasurable, boundless Ganges Rivers, so that they all come to my presence and receive what I offer.

Bestowing the unobstructed, pure food of the Dharma in an unrestricted manner as described in the sutras, each person received seventy-seven *droṇas* of food—the measure used in the kingdom of Magadha—and was individually satiated without any deficiency.

All their long-accumulated suffering of hunger, thirst, and being hung upside down was instantly extinguished; with bodies and minds filled with joy, they resolved upon Bodhicitta, and at that very moment—

May they attain the Samādhi of Mental Joy, swiftly cast off their ghostly bodies, be born in the Buddha’s Pure Land, quickly perfect the Wisdom of All Modes, and extensively deliver all sentient beings.

As the World-Honored One has said, this merit of my offering of food is no different from making offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Ganges-sands of Buddhas, the Truly Equally Awakened Ones. May this merit be dedicated to the adornment of the Dharma-realm.
May this bodhicitta vow be fulfilled together with all sentient beings through the perfection of dāna-pāramitā;

may we distance ourselves from all the hunger and thirst of saṃsāra and swiftly attain the two unsurpassed fruits of ultimate bodhi and nirvāṇa; and may we bestow upon sentient beings the inexhaustible food of the Dharma.

The ritual for offering food is the same as the previously described method of offering food. One should follow the sūtra; the text can be consulted there, so there is no need to set it out separately.

If one wishes to personally recite mantras, one may do so according to one's own intellectual capacity. If one does not wish to do so at all, one simply holds the food with the left hand while using the right hand [to perform the rite].
Chant the mantra over the vessel seven times and snap your fingers seven times; then pour the food onto clean ground, and it will suffice.
Simply give rise to the thought of offering, for by the power of the mantra, this water and food shall be inexhaustible.

As for the names of the four outer Tathāgatas and the four mantras listed below, use whichever you can; whether for public duties, private affairs, or for long-term preservation, employ them as appropriate.
It is sufficient to recite this single mantra seven times over the food, and all will be fully provided. According to the translation by Shichaya, there is only this one mantra;
the four Tathāgatas and others are not included. For those who practice this rite of Bestowing Food (*śrāddha*), I wish they would follow the ancient models.
Fearing that they may still be unfamiliar with the details, I have specially transcribed this for them. Repeatedly shown by the Śramaṇa Zunshi.
Homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions. Homage to the Dharma of the ten directions. Homage to the Sangha of the ten directions.
Homage to the Greatly Compassionate Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. (Recite three times.
Through the empowerment of this divine mantra, may these pure offerings of food and drink be universally bestowed upon all spirits and deities as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
May all be fully satisfied and abandon their stinginess; May they immediately escape the dark realms and be reborn in the good paths.
Taking refuge in the Triple Gem and training in Bodhicitta, May they ultimately attain unsurpassed enlightenment.
With boundless merit extending to the end of the future, May all sentient beings partake equally in the Dharma-food.
Namo sarva-tathāgate vairocanate | Oṃ sambhara sambhara hūṃ | (Recite seven times) | Namo Ratnasaṃbhavāya Tathāgatāya | Namo Suvarṇavarṇāya Tathāgatāya.
Homage to the Tathāgata Vipula-kāya. Homage to the Tathāgata Vigatabhaya. (Recite each three times.
You hosts of spirits and deities, I now bestow this offering upon you. May this food reach all spirits and deities throughout the ten directions.
May we together vow that by this merit, it shall extend universally to all; may I and all sentient beings together attain the Way of the Buddha.
(Having spoken thus, snap the fingers seven times and perform the gift of fearlessness; then pour the food onto the clean ground and visualize that all ghosts and spirits eat it).
Regarding the visualization for the offering of food (*śrāddha*): (In response to the questions of Cui Yucái, Director of the Bureau of Topography).

This is similar to the previous [method]; first, briefly describe the general meaning, and then perform the visualization. First, to describe the general meaning: the food and drink possess color, fragrance, and flavor.
Regarding the dharma of touch, among the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), sound alone is absent; yet among these five objects, the object of taste (*rasa*) is predominant.
Taste abides in form (*rūpa*), and thus one may also contemplate form as the objective realm. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Within form there is no characteristic of taste;

ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) should not be attached to it, and those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayānika*) should not seek to abandon it. This very state—neither taste nor abandonment—is the Dharma of the Middle Way within manifest color (*varṇa-rūpa*).
What dharma is not contained within the realms? Therefore, a single form possesses all forms, as well as all sensory objects such as sounds and fragrances, and all dharmas and all minds;
they are manifested according to one's karmic conditions. What dharma does not appear? As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"For example, when the various devas eat from a common precious vessel, the color of the rice differs according to their respective merit. This is the Great [Meaning] of Stopping and Contemplation.
Regarding the "wondrous realm of the mind," it is said: within each and every atom there are all atoms; within each and every atom there are all minds;
within each and every mind there are all lands, and so forth. The *Vyākhyā* (Śāstra) states:

"When a Bodhisattva refutes the perception of form and perceives the true reality of form, reaching the other shore of form, this is seeing the Middle Way within form. If one discriminates form as possessing various characteristics, this is [seeing the conventional]."
Form is the conventional truth; the conventional is emptiness, which is the seeing of form as the ultimate truth. Thus, one sees form through the three truths.

Once these three truths are understood—namely, that form is the dharma-realm, the true mark, and the middle way—one should realize that the equality of the three truths means form itself is the dhāraṇī.
You should know that the color and flavor of the food and drink offered are themselves the dhāraṇī.
The essence (*tattva*) is that from a single meal, immeasurable food emerges; this is the function (*vṛtti*) of the *dhāraṇī*. The Sūtra says:
"This *dhāraṇī* is named 'Infinite Majestic Virtue, Sovereign Radiance, and Supreme Wondrous Power'. Furthermore, its meaning is established through three virtues:
"infinite majestic virtue" refers to the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*); "radiance" refers to the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā*); and "supreme wondrous power" refers to the *dharmakāya*.

"Virtue" and "power" are a summary of the functioning of power. If it were not for the supreme and wondrous function of the Dharma-body, how could a single meal satisfy a multitude of beings as numerous as the sands of billions of worlds? Question:
If "I" am identical to the *dhāraṇī*, why is it still necessary to recite incantations? Answer: It is indeed so; the Buddhas and holy sages realize this single atom as the Dharma-realm.
Therefore, being able to employ the power of mastery in accordance with the nature of reality, why wait for further incantations?
When Vimalakīrti took a single bowl of fragrant rice and satisfied thirty-two thousand people without anything lacking, how could this have relied upon incantations?

Those of the Three Vehicles, sages and saints alike, who eat this food all enter the stage of correctness, or increase their realization and diminish their remaining births; only when the fragrance has vanished does it disappear—is this not indeed [the case]?

All dharmas are thus; it is only because sentient beings are deluded that they are confused regarding principle and obstructed regarding phenomena within the dharma of self-mastery, thereby binding themselves as if water were frozen into ice—how then can one blame the water for its lack of function?

Therefore, the Sage employs skillful means to secretly teach this dharma, naming it *dhāraṇī*, commanding that it be recited as a mantra; the syllables of the mantra are identical in nature to form, flavor, and the nature of all dharmas.
It should be able to cause ghosts and spirits to see the food. The *Wuliang jing* (Sūtra of Immeasurable Life) says:

"It is like a person obtaining one *jin* of mineral flux that transforms a thousand *jin* of copper into gold; this is because the natures and characteristics of things resonate with one another. Question:

In the section on the formal title of the *Shishi* (Offering of Food), it states that each of the six realms possesses its own inherent power, yet only ghosts are able to transform food. Why not simply provide them with the food directly, allowing them to take it as they please?
"Why rely on mantras for transformation? Answer: There are many kinds of ghosts, which need not all be treated as one; briefly stated, there are three categories.

First, the *niṣkiñcana* (destitute) ghosts, who, due to a lack of merit, do not obtain food or drink. Second, the *alpakiñcana* (possessing little) ghosts, who obtain a small amount of pure and exquisite food and drink.
Third, the *bahukiñcana* (possessing much) ghosts, who obtain a great deal of pure and exquisite food and drink. Furthermore, regarding these three categories...
Each of these has three types; first, the "wealthless" ghosts (*preta*). Regarding these three: first, the "torch-mouthed" ghosts (*ulkāmukha*), whose mouths constantly emit blazing torches of fire.
Second, the "needle-throated" ghosts (*sūcīmukha*), whose bellies are as large as mountains while their throats are like the eye of a needle.

It is specifically for these two types that this sutra speaks, though it also includes all others by extension. Third, the "stench-mouthed" ghosts (*durgandhamukha*), whose mouths are foul with putrid stench, which they themselves loathe.
Regarding those who suffer from little wealth, there are also three kinds of *piśāca* spirits: first, the needle-haired spirits, whose hair is as sharp as needles and which pricks them as they move;

second, the foul-haired spirits, whose hair is like thorns and which they must pluck out themselves, thereby suffering pain; third, the goitered spirits, who have large goiters hanging from their throats which they must tear open themselves to consume the pus.
Regarding those with much wealth, there are also three kinds: first, the spirits who receive discarded offerings, meaning they constantly obtain sacrificial offerings.
First are the ghosts who subsist on discarded food from sacrifices; second are those who gain or lose, meaning they constantly obtain food left behind in streets and alleys;
third are the powerful ghosts, such as yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas, whose enjoyment of wealth and pleasure resembles that of humans and devas, though they are categorized among the evil destinies.
As for what is called "transformable food," it refers to the three types within the category of those with abundant wealth.

Furthermore, among the three types of ghosts, the first two are inferior while the latter one is superior; yet even they can only reach their own kind and are unable to provide broad relief to others.
Now, through the power of this mantra’s transformation, it enables all nine types of ghosts to equally obtain exquisite food and drink without any distinction.
Moreover, that which is called "mantra-food" is known as "Dharma-food," for the Dharma follows the food.
Entering [this state] is like taking excellent medicine that can cure a grave illness, whereby the body becomes healthy and one experiences bliss.
As the Sūtra says, "Having abandoned the body of a hungry ghost, one attains birth in the heavens"—this is precisely the meaning. Second, regarding the practice of visualization (*bhāvanā*):

once the practitioner has realized that all phenomena are nothing other than the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), where the one and the many are mutually unimpeded, and having further gained faith in the inconceivable power of the *dhāraṇī*, they proceed to the offering of food (*piṇḍapāta*).
Standing in a place of tranquility, first arouse a mind of loving-kindness and compassion for those suffering from hunger and thirst.

Thinking, "I now intend to perform a great act of giving," first visualize that place as vast, pure, and adorned; its ground level and even, serving as a field of giving capable of accommodating an immeasurable multitude of hungry ghosts.
Next, visualize the vessels for food, which, through the power of my mantra, become like the great *droṇa* measures of the Magadha kingdom.

Visualize that within each vessel, delicious food and drink fill it to the brim like celestial nectar; these vessels become immeasurable, filling the entire field of giving until it is completely packed.

Before every single hungry ghost, imagine your own body appears; reciting the mantra, snapping your fingers, and extending your arm with a compassionate heart, you hand over the vessel and bestow it upon them, satisfying them according to their wishes.
Imagine that the sound of the mantra is heard everywhere and the sound of the finger-snapping reaches all beings.
The sound awakens all the hungry ghosts dwelling in dark and secluded places; they come from the four directions without obstruction to receive the food before them.
One should cause their thoughts and minds to become clear and vivid, as if seeing with their own eyes.

Then, without shifting this visualization, one should preach the Dharma for each of them individually, either by reciting the Buddha’s name or by offering incantations and vows, doing as one pleases. Having finished, one withdraws. Question:
Regarding the basis for the aforementioned visualization, this scripture, though concise, does not explicitly state it;

however, one must follow the visualizations for the mantras and mudrās according to other mantra sections, performing them with each successive phrase of the mantra without a single moment’s deviation.

For this mantra as well, one should press the vessel with the hand and recite the mantra seven times; having finished the recitation, snap the fingers seven times—it is not that no ritual action is performed at all.
Now, adding visualization further increases its efficacy. Question: On what basis is this sequence for arranging the ritual path and performing the visualizations established?
Answer: It is based on the "Contemplation of Successive Phenomena" (*lishi guan*) among the three types of contemplation taught by Tiantai.

Since it is said that one establishes visualization according to the specific characteristics of each phenomenon, in the section on impermanence, we now follow Tiantai’s practice of offering to the Triple Gem by manifesting incense and flowers.

The essential principle of visualization is the same [as previously described]. Furthermore, the *Gāthā on the Contemplation of Food* by Master Nanyue says: "The color and fragrance of this food are like the scent of sandalwood;
in a single moment, they universally permeate the worlds of the ten directions. All sentient beings, whether mundane or sagely, who have a karmic affinity, each obtain the supreme flavor.
Those in the six realms who smell this fragrance give rise to the bodhicitta. Through this food, one can produce the six pāramitās as well as the three types of practice."
Please examine this contemplation carefully; why wait for doubt to arise? Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states:

"One should offer a single meal to all beings, making offerings to all Buddhas and worthy sages, and only then may one eat. Is this not the contemplation of food? Question: Since the transformation of food is brought about by the power of mantras, what need is there for contemplation?

Answer: Contemplation supports the mantra, further enhancing its efficacy. Moreover, the mantra is the power of another, whereas contemplation is one's own power. Thus, the two are mutually reinforcing.
This is the power of one's own strength: merely reciting mantras without visualization is like a blind person who asks another to hold a great assembly for giving;

though they trust the other’s words, saying "I have received food" or "I have not received food," they never see it for themselves at all. If visualization is added, it is like a person with sight who asks another to hold a great assembly for giving;
they see every detail with their own eyes, not relying on the words of another. Thus, the mantra is like the act of having someone perform the visualization.
As seen in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "If a bodhisattva dwells upon dharmas while practicing giving, it is like a person entering darkness who sees nothing.
If one practices giving without dwelling upon dharmas, it is like a person with eyes who, when the light of the sun shines, sees various forms.
Now, to practice merely as a matter of duty without contemplation is like a person entering darkness.

To contemplate that what is called the Dharma-realm is non-abiding is itself the practice of non-abiding giving; its merit is like the empty space of the ten directions, inconceivable and immeasurable.

If one can perform such contemplation when engaging in any Buddha-activity—even offering a single flower or a single incense stick—one will not be obstructed by birth and death, and every stream of action will flow into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Even a small amount of precept-keeping or a small amount of giving [becomes infinite through this contemplation].
That all shall attain the fruit of Buddhahood is truly due to this.
*A Eulogy on Resolving Doubts through Reforming Sacrifices and Cultivating the Pure Fast* (with preface), as before.

Recently, I have observed many who reform sacrificial rites and compete to cultivate the merit of the pure fast; they abstain from meat and cease killing, maintaining right mindfulness and reciting the Buddha’s name—this is most excellent.

It is rare indeed that, amidst these circumstances, some who do not understand the benefits or harms of such practices will recklessly give rise to slander and destruction, claiming either that for laypeople sacrificial offerings come first, or that fasting and precepts cannot save one in times of urgency.
Upon seeing those who practice vegetarianism and recite the Buddha’s name, they say, "I merely maintain my own mind;

as for the causes and conditions of good and evil that lead to future lives, who is it that receives them? Consequently, many whose roots of goodness are not yet deep become confused and disturbed by such views.
Having withdrawn from my initial draft, I now provide scriptural citations and clear evidence to sever doubts, and compose verses for easy memorization.
Relying on these sincere words, do not believe in heterodox teachings. However, because worldly people harbor suspicions, I shall now briefly record ten verses according to the essentials.
First, there is doubt as to whether ghosts exist and whether they can bring about calamity or fortune.
The commentary states: The sūtras speak of the six realms of existence, and ghosts constitute one of them; how can you doubt that ghosts do not exist? The Āgama Sūtra says:
"All dwellings, houses, streets, alleys, lanes, slaughterhouses, marketplaces, as well as mountains and burial mounds, are all..."
There are spirits and deities, yet they can neither benefit nor harm people. The *Piyu jing* (Sutra of Parables) states:
"The spirits and deities of the world cannot bring life to the living, nor can they kill; they cannot make people wealthy or poor.

They merely manifest strange portents and disturbances according to a person's decline or inferiority, hoping for offerings and sacrifices. If one seeks blessings from them, there will certainly be none. This is the worldly view.
Unaware that one is being deceived, people kill living beings and commit evil deeds. A verse says:
"Gods and spirits exist everywhere, Deceiving the people of the world; In making offerings, there is no merit at all, Only increasing the causes for karmic retribution through killing."
Second, there is the doubt that one observes people in the world who obtain peace through sacrifices during illness; why then do you say there is no merit? The explanation states:
For people in the world, poverty, calamities, and blessings all belong to the realm of cause and effect, and cannot be brought about by ghosts.

That ghosts provide blessings is merely what is summoned by false faith and obtained through sycophantic seeking. As the *Vādavidhi* (Treatise on Distinguishing Right and Wrong) says: "Old ghosts instruct new ones."
A ghost and a demon went to two households in search of food; they turned the millstones and operated the pestle for them.

The families were followers of the Buddha and did not believe in such things, yet both said, "It is a benevolent deity who assists us," and though they pounded and ground several *hu* of rice and wheat all day long, they could not obtain any food at all.
Later, [the spirits] entered a household that believed in heterodox ways and caused a white dog to walk through the air above it; the family was greatly terrified.
By killing a dog and preparing a meal, one may thereby obtain satisfaction; you should know that to have faith in the Buddha does not require believing in the strange.
Even if you encounter something strange, simply focus exclusively on reciting the Buddha’s name, and that strangeness will naturally subside. The verse says:

When one possesses right faith, devas and nāgas will protect them; how could malevolent spirits possibly prevail? If one simply knows to constantly recollect the Buddha, calamities and anomalies will naturally dissipate.
Third, regarding the doubt: after family members have died, do their offerings receive food or not?

The commentary states: If one falls among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), at the time of a sacrificial offering, some may obtain food, while those who are "flame-mouthed" (*yāmukha*) ghosts cannot obtain food even if a sacrifice is performed.

The *Āgama* Sūtra says: "If one performs offerings and sacrifices for the sake of the deceased, if the deceased has entered the realm of hungry ghosts, they will obtain the food; if they have been reborn in another place, they will certainly not obtain it. (6)
The myriad species receive retributions that differ from one another; when parents die, how could they all necessarily become ghosts?
That people do not recognize this and instead perform sacrifices exclusively is utterly irrational. The verse says:

When a person dies, they follow their prior karma, rising or sinking through the six realms with their destinies diverging. How can one say that those who perform only sacrifices are ignorant of the Way?

This is the fourth doubt. Regarding the methods of sacrifice, they are extensively detailed in the Ritual Classics (*Lijing*): the Son of Heaven has seven ancestral temples, while the feudal lords have five.
Now, from the high ministers down to the common people, all alike perform sacrifices at the Round Mound and the Square Pond to worship the spirits of heaven and earth;
this is the eternal statute of the state. Why then do you urge them to cease these sacrifices? It would cause great injury to the national spirit!
The commentary states: Sacrifices originate from secular scriptures, while the cessation of sacrifice is based on the Buddhist sutras.
Secular scriptures do not escape the taking of life; the Buddhist sutras, however, esteem only compassion. If one takes life, the retribution lies within the three miserable realms (*trāya*);

if one practices compassion, the fruit is the perfection of the myriad virtues. Using goodness to reform evil and guiding the shallow toward the profound, there are no sentient beings whom the Buddha does not deliver.

Now that you people have already placed faith in the Buddha-dharma, you must cultivate the compassion of the Buddha and must no longer kill sentient beings while claiming to be disciples of the Buddha;
how much more so when, according to current customs, you not only sacrifice to your ancestors but worship every deity without exception—this is what is called licentious sacrifice.

To fail to cultivate bright virtue and instead devote oneself solely to killing living beings is a tragedy of the deepest kind, which cannot be fully expressed in brief discourse. Thus it was in the past, under Emperor Wu of Liang...
The Emperor issued an edict throughout the realm to cease sacrifices and stop killing; this was surely in accordance with the Buddhist teachings, not only today.
It is fortunate that there is the merit of the fast, which is precisely the time to compete in cultivation; it can benefit both the living and the deceased, and also spare the lives of creatures.
Why labor under the burden of adhering to sacrificial rites? The verse says: [Verse omitted as per instructions]
The sacrificial oxen feel shame at the *yue* offerings; the millet and grain are inherently not fragrant.
When one recites the true and bright virtue in purity, why labor over the ritual classics? (5) Question: What karmic retribution do those who perform sacrifices and the shamans obtain?
The commentary states: As explained in the Vinaya-vibhaṅga, Kālatīya—an Arhat who had attained bodily realization—was killed by the wife of a Brahmin.
This was because he had previously served as a sacrificial master for a temple shrine.
Furthermore, five hundred merchants once slaughtered a single sheep together and came to offer prayers; having killed the sheep for sacrifice, they all subsequently fell into hell.
Throughout successive lifetimes, he has repeatedly been slaughtered as a sheep; those five hundred men were likewise killed by King Prasenajit because of that same woman.

Furthermore, when five hundred people together kill a single life along with its presiding sacrificer, they now testify to the fruits of the Path, yet their retribution remains unfinished—how much more so for one person who kills the lives of many creatures? Moreover, during the Jin dynasty, at Baqiu County...
There was a shaman named Li of the Shu clan who performed sacrifices for others; after he died, he fell into the Hell of Burning and Slaying, where his entire body was scorched and withered.

Upon returning to life, he recounted his experience. Furthermore, the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* extensively explains the retribution for performing sacrifices, which cannot be cited here in full. A verse says:
To kill another is to kill oneself; like shadow and echo following form and sound, when ghosts are satiated there is no merit, and one vainly invites a fall into the fiery pit.
Regarding the sixth doubt: if one were to change the sacrificial rites now, has there ever been a recorded response or verification from ancient times?
The commentary states: Instances of such spiritual efficacy are not limited to one; I shall now briefly cite an example from the Jin dynasty involving Zhang Ying.
His family worshipped local deities and engaged in licentious sacrifices. In the eighth year of the Xianhe era, his wife fell ill, and he exhausted his resources in prayers and offerings for her.

His wife said, "My illness grows more severe each day; praying to spirits is of no benefit. I beg you to perform Buddhist rites. Ying immediately consented and invited the monk Tan-kai to preside over them.

While Zhang Ying was preparing for a vegetarian feast, he dreamed that a divine being reproached him for not having made the preparations pure and solemn enough. Seeing Zhang Ying following behind, the deity said, "He has only just begun to resolve his mind toward awakening;

you should not yet reproach him. Upon waking, Ying kept a lamp burning throughout the night and prepared the seats for the feast. From then on, he abandoned his service to the spirits and devoted himself to the Buddha.
Later, after his wife’s illness had been cured, Zhang Ying died and fell into the Hell of Boiling Cauldrons because he had previously failed to serve the spirits.
He sacrificed to the benevolent deity who came to rescue him, whereupon he attained liberation; returning to life, he recounted the events himself.

During the era of Emperor Wu of the Great Liang, when the governance was pure and the Way brought benefit to all within the realm, warfare was forever stilled. The Emperor solely revered Buddhist principles;

his life was one of leisure and ease. He wore straw sandals and a ramie cap, used a cloth quilt and a mat of *guǎn* grass, and strictly observed the fasts and precepts to provide relief and succor to all living beings.
With compassion for the four debts of gratitude, his mind was focused upon the three realms of existence; day and night he burned incense and recited scriptures without a moment’s pause.

Consequently, he moved the sages and worthies to jointly support the state. Suddenly, in the middle of the night, he dreamed of a high monk of pure spirit and ancient appearance, with snow-white hair and thick eyebrows, who addressed the Emperor, saying:
"The six paths and four modes of birth suffer immeasurably; there is a vast land-and-water *mingzhai* (esoteric vegetarian feast) in the world."
Among all meritorious deeds that universally save sentient beings and bring benefit and joy to those in both the hidden and manifest realms, this is the most preeminent;
it is fitting to prepare offerings with reverence. Once the Emperor was awakened by this realization, he ascended to court at dawn and personally attended the precious hall.

He immediately questioned his great ministers and various śramaṇas regarding the matter of the dream concerning water and land, but none knew anything of it. Only Master Zhi submitted, saying: "I only beg Your Majesty..."
Having extensively sought out the scriptural teachings, [the Emperor] realized there must have been a specific cause and condition;

accordingly, he submitted a memorial and immediately dispatched an envoy to welcome the Tripitaka of sutras and śāstras, which were placed in the Fayun Hall. Over many days, he perused them and thoroughly investigated their origins.

Furthermore, upon examining in detail how Ānanda encountered the Ghost King with a Scorched Face and established the "Equal Measure" (Pingdeng hu) of food based on his past causes, he composed the ritual texts, completing them in three years. During that interval...

Having obtained eleven texts of sutras and treatises that fully encompassed the essential matters, his mind still harbored doubts: first, fearing that the Sage’s intention might not have been fully expressed;
second, fearing that the common understanding of the masses might not yet be satisfied. Thereupon, he once again prepared the inner quarters and specially established a *dharmāśālā*.
As night approached, he personally attended the Dharma assembly, kneeling to pay his respects and holding the ritual texts in his hands. He then looked toward his attendants and said:
Your servant extinguished the lamps and candles, leaving all in darkness; the Emperor then reverently burned incense and made a vow, recounting his dream and composing this text for the ritual.

If its principles accord with the sacred and the mundane, and its benefits extend to both the unseen and the manifest, may the lamps at the site where the prostrations were performed shine by themselves without being heated.

The candles all became dark and dim; having finished speaking, he prostrated himself on the ground. Once the prostrations were completed, the lamps and candles shone brightly once more.
When the Emperor beheld this, his countenance was filled with great joy. Thereupon, wishing to establish this fast, he summoned Master Zhi to ask where it should be held.

By the Longlu Bhikṣu Zongze, regarding the origins of the Water and Land Assembly:
As for the Water and Land Assembly, at its highest level, it makes offerings to all Buddhas of the Dharma-realm and to the various classes of Bodhisattvas and Pratyekabuddhas.
One makes offerings to the Śrāvakas, the Vidyārājas, the eight classes of spirits, and the Brahmanical sages;

next, to Brahmā, Śakra, the twenty-eight celestial deities, all the lunar mansions and planets throughout space, and all honored spirits; below these, one makes offerings to the dragon deities of the five sacred peaks, rivers, seas, and the great earth;
and finally, to the ancient human beings, the hosts of asuras, the retinues of the underworld officials, and the sentient beings and ghostly souls in the hells.

For those lingering spirits who have no master and no refuge, for the multitudes of ghosts and gods, the various beings of the dharma-realm, the animals of the six paths, and those in the intermediate state—both the four classes of noble ones and the six categories of ordinary beings—I universally offer this Dharma-food through the merit of the Tathāgata’s secret divine mantras.

Thus, externally it sustains the body, increasing physical vigor and strength; internally it sustains the spirit, increasing merit and wisdom. By means of this, those who have not yet awakened their bodhicitta...

Those who have resolved their minds toward enlightenment (bodhicitta) do so because of this supreme assembly of water and land beings; those not yet liberated from the wheel of suffering do so because of it and attain non-retrogression;
and those who have not yet realized the Buddha-way do so because of this supreme assembly of water and land beings and attain the Buddha-way.

If making offerings to a single Buddha, providing a meal for a single monk, giving alms to a single poor person, or encouraging a single person toward goodness still possesses infinite merit, how much more so [is this assembly]?

How much more so when making general offerings to the Triple Gem of the ten directions, the six paths of existence, and the myriad spirits—how could this merely benefit one’s own person to transcend the three realms alone?

It is such that its grace moistens the nine ancestral generations, its blessings extend to both the hidden and the manifest, and it equally delivers all sentient beings to the same attainment of the Buddha-way;
it may truly be called a great ocean of merit, incalculable, countless, immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.
Therefore, the Water and Land Buddhist rites have flourished throughout the ages across the Yangtze and Huai rivers, the two Zhe provinces, Sichuan, Guangxi, and Fujian, whether by water or land.

If one seeks to ensure peace and prosperity yet does not perform the Water and Land rites, people consider it improper; if one wishes to provide for the posthumous merit of one's elders yet does not perform the Water and Land rites, people consider it unfilial;
and if one intends to deliver one’s juniors from suffering yet does not perform the Water and Land rites, people [consider it...]
Thinking that this lack of compassion arose from this [principle], the wealthy prepared the offerings with their own resources alone, while the poor pooled their wealth to perform the rites;

the miraculous responses resulting therefrom cannot be fully recounted. Fearing that the people of this region may not yet know the origins of these matters, I have now set forth the history of the Water and Land (Shuilu) rites below.
