When a lotus emerges from the mud, defilements cannot adhere to it; for this reason, one should give rise to the bodhicitta as the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Second, one must give rise to a vast and expansive mind as the assembly of the Dharma (*dharmasamāja*);

one should reflect that this mind is inherently free of discrimination and equal to space, yet it is merely obscured by ignorance, hindered by worldly desires, and gives rise to the notion of a self (*ātman*).
Seeing that I conceived thoughts of enmity toward my kin, I caused the Tathāgata to enter parinirvāṇa while I was born in another realm where I could not see a Buddha;
it is only today, at this very moment, that I must repent and cleanse myself, giving rise to a vast and great mind.
Just as the moon does not leave the sky and its reflection appears wherever there is water, by these causes and conditions, one should employ a vast body.
Third, within this Dharma assembly of the mind, one must first give rise to the heart of great vows as an offering. One should reflect:

"Boundless sentient beings have never yet been delivered; I shall now deliver them all. Those sentient beings who have not yet attained the realization of the fruit, I shall now cause them to realize it.
All sentient beings of the six paths and four modes of birth, I shall ferry across and bring to the sages and worthies throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time."
To cause the substance of this practice to pervade everywhere, one must now, at this very moment, give rise to such a great vow-mind;

because the Dharma is inexhaustible, the offering is likewise inexhaustible. Fourth, one must give rise to a heart of great compassion as the wealth of the Dharma, reflecting that sentient beings commit various evil karmas, and by virtue of these evil karmas, they transmigrate into the evil realms. First.
Entering the evil realms without respite—if anyone should wish for me to take upon myself the various sufferings and afflictions of all sentient beings, I would not grant such a request.
Instead, within those very realms, I shall exhort and transform them to arouse the resolve for enlightenment, causing their minds to turn toward the good.
Furthermore, this very day and at this very hour, one must again give rise to this great compassionate mind and practice the gift of Dharma, bestowing it upon all sentient beings.
To leave suffering behind and attain happiness—if one can firmly give rise to these four kinds of great resolve, then one will know that this assembly is not like other assemblies;
it is the Tathāgata’s most supreme, unobstructed, and unimpeded gate of great liberation.
Therefore, I now cultivate the Great Fast for the spirits of land and water to gather immeasurable and boundless merit. Now, at this time...

Entering the Dharma Assembly: First, for the sake of the donors (*dānapati*), the people who have joined the ritual site (*maṇḍala*), and the sentient beings of the Dharma-realm—whether hidden or manifest, whether spiritual or ordinary—who rely upon the sacred teachings, there are four kinds of vast body and mind; regarding this, there is a mantra, which says... [and so forth].
The Proclamation for Inviting the Eight Holy Beings to Ascend the Dharma Seat, as before:
We have heard that the Great Hero appeared in the world to provide protection and refuge for all sentient beings; that the wondrous Dharma serves as a guiding principle to deliver and liberate all.
Performing rare and marvelous deeds, he opens the gate of great compassion and surveys the fourfold assembly with the majestic turn of an elephant king, unfolding his teachings...
With a single voice, he utters the lion’s roar without rising from his precious lotus throne;
he universally transforms the ten directions and constantly emits the light of the jade-hair mark, illuminating the six realms of existence.

He spreads the clouds of compassion throughout the Dharma-realm and pours down the nectar of immortality upon all living beings—the King among the sages of the human realm, the Great Compassionate Father of the world. Tonight, there is a disciple named [Name]. Only...

I reflect that from vast eons past until this present life, I have received the great kindness of the Buddha; fortunately, I have heard the Buddha’s true teaching and am sheltered by the universal protection of the Triple Gem.
Yet I lament the drifting of beings through the six realms—how can one encounter a Buddha, who is as rare as a turtle meeting a floating log?
Looking back at my own body, it possesses the treasure of clothing, yet I remained unaware of it. From one body to the next, I pass from suffering into further suffering. Now...
I wish to guide them along the path of liberation and advance them through the gateway of skillful means; may the Buddha, out of compassion, fulfill my aspirations.
For this reason, I present these humble yet exquisite vegetarian offerings and universally arrange these rare incense and flowers.
My devotion is unsurpassed, my sincerity is profound, and my intent is sincere; therefore, on behalf of the donor, I now respectfully and earnestly invite you to ascend.
The eight venerable members of the assembly in this hall, we humbly entreat you to descend upon us. We, the assembly of Buddhāya,
with one mind take refuge and pay homage, inviting the True Dharma, the Ocean of Nature, and the Wondrous Reward and Transformation Bodies, adorned with the majesty of myriad virtues.
Pervading the ten directions with sovereign mastery, you transcend all names and marks, realizing that there is neither difference nor identity across the three periods of time.

You engage with the defilements of the world, appearing or remaining hidden for the sake of all living beings. Your compassionate light is immeasurable and your vows of mercy inexhaustible—vast as the great ocean from which Mount Sumeru emerges, and bright as the myriad stars that depend upon the full moon. Homage to the Infinite One, who pervades the void and the entire Dharma-realm. (1)
I pray that the assembly of the eternally abiding Buddha-tathāgatas, not departing from the equality of the primordial limit (*ādikoti*) and permeated by universal compassion,
will deign to descend to this site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and accept these offerings. I further entreat the assembly of the Dharma.
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge, pay homage, and entreat you: You who manifest the ten thousand images of the nature-heaven and the myriad waves of the Dharma-ocean;

you who open the gates of the vast meaning of Vairocana and illuminate the profound treasure-trove of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); you who carry all beings in the three vehicles beyond the village of the burning house;

you who respond to capacities through the eight teachings, causing them all to enter the net of the celestial pearl; you who clearly reveal the provisional and the real, showing that even the fish-trap and rabbit-snare are ultimately empty—homage to you, who are so praised by all!
The supreme field of merit is the boundless, true gift of Dharma; *namo* to the assembly of all eternally abiding Dharmas that pervade the inexhaustible void of the Dharma-realm.
I entreat the assembly of the Saṃgha to with one mind take refuge and pay homage, to uphold the purity of the six harmonies and the perfect luminosity of the single nature;

to adorn the body with the precepts and to gather sentient beings through compassion and patience; to pour forth eloquent discourse like the ocean, skillfully proclaiming the Dharma-gates of all the sages; and to reflect the moon of meditative concentration.
With a lofty mind, one reveals the true eye of a thousand wondrous opportunities; unstained by a single speck of dust, one does not violate the myriad practices.

With the crown of the head rounded by the secret pearl of Samādhi, a radiant body hangs with the nine-fold auspicious numinous herbs. Homage to the inexhaustible Saṃgha of all those who eternally abide throughout the pervasive realm of empty space.

I entreat the assembly of Great Bodhisattvas to single-mindedly take refuge, pay homage, and make this invocation: may you give rise to great vows, aspire toward Great Bodhi, advance through the stages of the six perfections,

realize the equality of the one true nature, and— through the four immeasurables of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity— master the mechanism of non-perception while entering and emerging from birth and death.
Not falling into the marks of sense organs or objects, the clouds of Potalaka are exquisite and the breezes of Tuṣita are pure;

with jeweled flowers and necklaces adorning their bodies, they are the luminosity of the ocean of the nature of reality, constantly benefiting all beings. *Namo* to the assembly of all Mahāsattva Bodhisattvas who dwell eternally throughout the inexhaustible void that pervades the Dharma-realm.

I entreat the assembly of great Pratyekabuddhas to single-mindedly take refuge, pay homage, and make this invocation: through the conditions of awakening, you have transcended the world; you have cultivated the path in solitude, dwelling eternally within mountain forests, never taking up verbal discourse.
Like deer, you carry others across, liberating them from the twelve links of existence; like rhinoceroses, you possess solitary horns.

Transcending and ascending, they give rise to contemplative practice; through forty-four kinds of wisdom, they secretly illumine the true emptiness, and their wondrous concentration is solitary and perfect.
Although they appear in worlds where no Buddha dwells, they take realization solely by means of the faculties of the Middle Vehicle.
*Namo* to the assembly of all eternally abiding *pratyekabuddhas*, who pervade the infinite, empty, and boundless *dharmadhātu*.

I entreat the assembly of Great Arhats to unite their minds in taking refuge, prostrating, and making this invocation: May you whose faculty of wisdom is utterly detached from the realm of meditative concentration, who are lofty and transcendent, swiftly surpassing the suffering wheel of the triple world;

who have deeply realized the wondrous principle of solitary emptiness and will not undergo further existence; who are like a bright mirror free from all dust—may you be fully endowed [with these qualities].

With supernatural powers resembling the manifestation of a bright pearl, you abide in the stages of the four fruits; your fame fills the ten directions, and all those in the human and celestial realms take refuge in you as one.
You are able to respond to the needs of thousands of households. Homage to the assembly of all eternally abiding Great Arhats, who pervade the infinite void and the entire Dharma-realm.

I entreat the assembly of immortals possessing the five supernatural powers to single-mindedly take refuge and offer this invocation: with bodies and minds free from desire and virtues surpassing those of men,

you who long for the pure dwelling amidst the mist and clouds, residing in the profound seclusion of mountains and seas, you who drift upon crane-chariots, shining with the cold brilliance of moonlight and dew.

The ethereal robes chase the celestial wind as their fragrance disperses; wondrously termed "leakless," they alone attain eternal life. Fire is divided into dragon and tiger, revealing the divine elixir;

waves surge as whales and turtles leap within the secret palace. Homage to the assembly of immortals with the five supernatural powers, who abide eternally throughout the infinite void that pervades the entire Dharma-realm.

I pray that the assembly of Dharma-protecting devas and nāgas will with one mind take refuge and offer this invocation: You who have accumulated all merit and possess great majestic power, having already ascended the gate of liberation, you reverently protect the teachings of the Tathāgata;
your robes and crowns shine resplendently, for which nothing is not sustained by the power of goodness, and your retinues are magnificently arrayed.
How could Vajrapāṇi ever be stained by the defilements of worldly toil? He constantly attends the assemblies of the Buddhas to subdue hostile māras;
his precious sword shines with the brilliance of Prajñā, and his banners of armor give forth the exquisite flames of Vajra.
Homage to the assembly of Dharma-protecting devas and nāgas, who dwell eternally within all liberation-gates that pervade the inexhaustible void of the Dharma-realm.
The Proclamation for the Invocation of the Eight Holy Beings and Worldly Spirits from Below:
Originally, the Way of the Spirits is not remote; one must know that through sincere devotion, the power of the sages is not distant, and prayers will surely be answered.
Whether in the brief span of a finger-snap or the instant of a fleeting turn, they may manifest as rain or auspicious colors, mingling with light clouds.
Amidst this confusion, where wealth and pack-horses drift like leaves carried by the wind, how could we have expected such radiant splendor and auspicious clouds?
We venture to hope that Your Holiness’s carriage will grant our humble request and accept this invitation.

I reverently invite the multitude of officials, functionaries, and attendants (Yang Yu’s original text contains only the titles for the invitation; the names of the various officials and their retinues, as well as the remainder, are supplemented here by this supplementary text).

With one mind, I reverently invite all officials, functionaries, and attendants throughout the entire dharma-realm—past and present, ancient and modern—including sovereigns, emperors, kings, lords, the hundred ministers, the thousand officials, and all classes of beings, each with their respective retinues and the common people, headed by the Sovereign.

As the governing authorities rely upon the common people for their administration, and as all lands under heaven have from time immemorial belonged to the King’s subjects, Emperor Wu of Liang established ceremonial protocols and the seating arrangements for his officials; thus, through the accumulation of virtuous causes in former lives, he now encounters this superior retribution:

possessing talent that unites both civil and military virtues, occupying a station where wealth and honor are fully realized, and bringing the nine provinces and the four seas under his transformative influence.

Among those nurtured within the myriad clans and the four classes of people, all have come under the banner of his command; favor and rejection depend on him alone, and his every movement follows his own whims.
Now that his power has departed and time has passed, his physical form has vanished while his retribution continues;

his grieving soul is dark and desolate, with no refuge for long kalpas, and the realm of the dead is gloomy and obscure, leaving him nowhere to dwell. May such officials and their subordinates alike take refuge in the Triple Gem.

Relying on the power of secret mantras, descend upon this ritual site and accept this unimpeded, vast offering (*kūṭāgāra*; *kūṭa* is pronounced as *bi-yi* [qie] meaning "lord," and *āgāra* is pronounced as *ru-er-shu* [qie] meaning "felt mat").

I entreat all the assemblies of devas throughout the three realms to, with one mind, reverently invite all the devas pervading the entire dharma-realm— the lords and kings of the heavens within the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, each together with their retinues— who,
due to their past causes of abiding in the six heavens of desire and observing the five precepts and ten wholesome deeds, have received their retributive dwellings.

Cultivating the nine stages of ascending tranquility and abiding in the eight meditative concentrations and four dhyānas, although his body remains subject to outflows (*āsrava*), his bliss is inexhaustible.
His majestic palace follows him, and its radiant light illuminates his person. With a lifespan of eighty-four thousand *kalpas*, this superior retribution is long-lasting;
yet, how can the cycle of birth and death within the twenty-five realms of existence ever come to an end? When the five signs of decay appear—
As if from a dream upon a pillow, they suddenly departed from the midst of the palaces and entered the realm of profound darkness; thus do the multitudes of the deva path all pray,
requesting the multitudes of the asura path.
With single-minded devotion, I invoke all the asura hosts throughout the entire dharma-realm— those with three heads and six arms, born through the five destinies and four modes of birth,

whether in the depths of the ocean or among the mountains— who, along with their retinues, have experienced the divergent retributions of past good and evil deeds; who harbor hearts of arrogance and contempt for others,
engage in acts of jealousy and suspicion, and because they were exclusively coarse and violent, have consequently received these hideous forms.
Some wear many heads as necklaces, while others have multiple arms sprouting from their shoulders; their bodies are like emerald lakes and their hair resembles golden elixir.
When manifesting a great body, they tower as high as Mount Sumeru; when displaying a minute form, they slink into the pores of a lotus fiber.
Though they could not prevail in battle against Śakra, they have already surrendered beneath the wheels of the Tathāgata; may they now restrain their wrath.
May their hearts be so transformed that their evil intentions are subdued; may all such hosts of asuras likewise be pacified.

We now, with a single mind, entreat all the human assemblies throughout the entire dharma-realm—whether noble or base, high or low, from the central lands to the border regions—to join in this invocation.

Their appearances are diverse and their forms distinct, each accompanied by their own retinues. Through the past practice of the five precepts, they now receive retribution within the nine realms of existence.

Being the spiritual essence of the myriad things, they are thus ranked among the Three Powers (Heaven, Earth, and Humanity). Some transcend the five paths of rebirth to reach the eight stages of meditative concentration;

others, attached to the five desires, fall into the three miserable realms. All this arises from the conditions of body and speech, leading to divergent paths of ascent and descent through the realms of sound, form, fragrance, and flavor.
Indulging in lust, dissipation, arrogance, and luxury, they lose their original mind at every moment and harbor deluded thoughts at every thought. A hundred years easily pass away;
failing to contemplate that sound and form are fundamentally empty, they find it difficult to leave behind even a single dream as they enter entirely the realms of saṃsāra.
May all such beings in the human realm share this aspiration.

I pray that the assembly of the hungry ghost realm will with one mind extend their invitation to all those in the hungry ghost realm throughout the entire Dharma-realm: those with scorched faces, fire-mouths, massive heads, and needle-thin throats;

those tormented by thirst and whose body hair stands on end like needles—each together with their retinues—from the seven afflictive emotions, following from the ten evil deeds across the nine classes of beings.
In the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, three general views are presented regarding the Yogācāra school. Ānanda saw them as faces, while Maudgalyāyana beheld them as flowers.
At the foot of Mount Cakravāḍa, one cannot exhaustively describe the hundreds of billions; by the banks of the Gaṅgā River, even citing grains of sand from the Ganges would not suffice.
There is nothing that does not have needles piercing their throats, their limbs burning with fire, and their bones groaning.
With the sound of broken carts, bellies as large as ruined jars, they lie upon their beds; they long for sweet nectar that never reaches them, tormented by the burning heat of afflictions,
their physical strength and vigor depleted by hunger, their forms hideous and loathsome— may all such hosts of hungry ghosts and all sentient beings who suffer from starvation be brought peace.

I entreat all beings in the realm of animals to join with one mind in this invocation: all those in the animal realm throughout the entire Dharma-realm— herds of fur-bearing creatures, flocks of winged birds, those that dwell in water or traverse the air,

those that nest or burrow, and even the most minute of bodies, each together with their kin and companions— dwell within the three realms and share in the four modes of birth, as numerous as motes of dust.
If the sands were beyond counting, none would fail to traverse the void, race across the wilds, ascend to heaven, or leap into the abyss; born from wombs, eggs, moisture, or transformation;
gathered in mountains, forests, rivers, and marshes; some many-legged or legless, some with flattened hair or coarse fur;
some possessing consciousness or lacking it; some minute in substance or vast in form—yet even those that fly amidst frost or gnaw wood are suddenly overtaken by calamity.
Trapped in nets, they cry out in grief; tossed by violent waves upon the void, they cannot escape being caught in the snares and traps.

Their resentment is severed upon the edge of knives and mortars, and their souls fly in terror amidst boiling water and fire. May all such beings of the animal realm [be released from] the *hu* (the fish-trap).

May the assembly of the hell realm, with one mind, extend this invitation to all beings within the hell realm throughout the entire Dharma-realm: those in the five *ānantarya* hells, those who have committed the ten grave offenses,
those in the eight hot and eight cold hells, each together with their retinues— those named and those not named in the hells, collectively known as the Iron City of *Niraya*.
Tall and vast, the vessels of immeasurable and boundless sin are ever more numerous, such that they are truly startling and terrifying.
These are divided into five hundred distinct compartments where beings undergo birth and death in vain;

within them, for a single day, they are seared by eighty-four thousand cauldrons of boiling brine and glowing coals, their bodies crushed and their bones shattered, while the towering heights of Sword-Tree and Blade-Mountain pierce their eyes and stab their hearts.
The wheel turns lightly upon the heavy, yet the retribution for karma remains manifest; like striking a stone or the mustard-seed city, when will there ever be rest?

Thus, for all beings within the hell realms and all sentient beings suffering internally and externally, may they [be spared from] being impaled (pronounced *zì*, with the initial *cī* and final *lì*).

I entreat all those outside the six realms to gather with one mind and offer this invocation to all beings outside the six realms throughout the entire Dharma-realm— those who have recently fallen from the three worlds,
or who have come from the five destinies; having entered between the two pillars of ascent and descent, they have traversed the paths of going and coming.
Within this intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one is bewildered and indistinct, shrouded in profound darkness and obscurity. Sometimes ascending, one’s head points toward the celestial palaces;
sometimes descending, one’s head turns toward the underworld. At times one hastens horizontally toward the south or north, or with feet directed toward the east or west.
Being wretched and inferior, one’s physical form is beyond description. Though one consumes sweet liquids, they remain unseen; one sustains oneself by inhaling the wind and drinking the dew.

Because we were formerly devoid of even a hair’s breadth of wholesome merit and adorned ourselves with [unwholesome] conduct, we have now received such karmic retribution; we now pray that both enemies and kin may be equally rescued, and that all beings, whether in the hidden or the manifest realms, may find sustenance.
Thus, for those outside the six destinies—the beings of the intermediate state—we likewise offer our vows.
Postscript to the Ritual Texts for the Water and Land Feast, following the same format as before.

According to the records of the Xiao family’s establishment of the Unrestricted (Mocā) Feast, its ritual procedures were extremely simple. Those currently in practice are all later generations who followed precedent and added embellishments to honor the Dharma;
yet, in the matter of ferrying beings across [to liberation], they are one and the same. I have humbly examined the intent of the Xiao family, which seems to have transcended the three realms.

Beyond this, those who have already entered the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*) are encompassed by the upper eight positions; those within the triple world who have not yet escaped the wheel of suffering are fully represented by the lower eight positions.

There is none among those who have entered the stage of the noble ones whom they do not honor, and there is none among those who have not escaped the wheel of suffering whom they do not rescue and deliver.
This is why it is called "unrestricted" (*aviśeṣa*). Furthermore, all things throughout the great earth are fundamentally equal to the Buddhas...
The Buddhas share a single source; the Tathāgatas themselves have never had any distinction between sentient beings and other realms.

It is only because of delusion regarding dependent origination that the true becomes obscured and ignorance gives rise to folly. Thus, one sits separated from the various sages and is deemed to follow a divergent path.

This text expounds the orthodox teaching and clarifies the fundamental conditions, revealing the mechanism for awakening and leading those who participate in this Dharma assembly toward the Dharma of liberation.
One attains success only after clearly perceiving that there is not a single thing upon the great earth that cannot become a Buddha.
Generally, for a vegetarian feast (*zhāi*), places where one can command the view of mountains and rivers and rely on dense forests are superior; the full moon day is the most auspicious date.

Three days prior to the ceremony, place pure water before the Buddha and maintain the recitation of mantras day and night, visualizing the water as nectar (*amṛta*) with which to sprinkle the *dharmabhakta* (sacred food). Thus...

The Tripitaka Master presides at the altar to proclaim the scriptures; his Buddhist service is that of the Dharma Master. As for the harmonious blending of sounds and the intermittent chanting of *brahman* hymns, this is the song of praise.
Holding the incense burner before the Holy One and silently mobilizing the power of aspiration, this is the role of the donor (*dānapati*).

Therefore, the donor must surely apply diligent and refined intent; only through such refined intent can one bring about spiritual resonance. The Dharma Master must, in turn, select [the appropriate practitioners].
Only after practicing lofty conduct can one honor the teachings; the Tripitaka must be firmly upheld, for only through right mindfulness can one draw upon the power of mantras.
One’s hymns of praise must be solemnized by sincerity, for only through sincerity can one perfect the Dharma assembly.

First, one should dwell in seclusion during the ritual fast to achieve purity; at the conclusion of the assembly, one should sit in meditation as if yearning for the Way. Each [participant] should act accordingly.
Only through complete devotion and reverence will one receive benefit for sentient beings; if one is not careful, it will result in no advantage and will not be protected by the sages and worthies.
Furthermore, there will be the reprimand of ghosts and spirits. I dare to inform the great assembly: let everyone be cautious regarding this!
The Petition for Invocation Prior to the *Hù* (Measures):

I have heard that the substance of the Great Perfect Mirror is not worn away by grinding nor blackened by dyeing; the King of Wish-Fulfilling Jewels is inexhaustible when taken and unfailing when used.
Alas, how is it that sentient beings, having lost their way since time immemorial, sink forever beneath the dark mountains and remain submerged?
Dragging their feet through the Yellow Springs, they establish their lives there; the light of wisdom does not illuminate them, and the fires of hunger burn eternally.

Though they may hear of the supreme vehicle of the Perfect and Sudden, they continue to taste bitter and foul flavors without end. Those of like nature gather together, and beings are divided by their kind;
wherever they dwell is a land of hardship and peril, and those with whom they associate are entirely envious, stingy, and greedy.
The multitude of true spirits, tigers, dragons, and snakes are as formidable as they are numerous, as abundant as rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds.

It is by the grace of the Dharma King’s provision of food offerings, and the fortune of the patrons’ adherence to the Tathāgata’s teachings, that at this clear night, incense and offerings are fully displayed.
May the spirits and ghosts rely on their own inherent power to provide for all needs, and may they be universally gathered through the unconditioned compassion of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

I have heard it said in the sūtras that in the past, when the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling alone in a quiet place, recollecting the teachings he had received, he saw at the dead of night a hungry ghost named Makhādeva (Face-Burning) who said to Ānanda:
"In three days' time, I shall meet my end and fall into the realm of hungry ghosts to become like you. Having heard this, Ānanda’s heart was filled with terror, and he questioned the hungry ghost.
The ghost said, "If after my death I am reborn as a hungry ghost, what skillful means may I employ to escape this state?
At that time, the hungry ghost addressed Ānanda, saying, "If you can give alms to hundreds of thousands of nayutas of hungry ghosts as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
as well as to hundreds of thousands of Brahmins and sages, each offering one *droṇa* measured by the Magadha standard, [I shall be liberated]."
"You shall obtain increased longevity through this food, while I shall attain liberation from suffering. Upon hearing these contrary words, Ānanda’s body hair stood on end.
He immediately went to where the Buddha was and related these words in detail: "World-Honored One, how can I now prepare such food for the various ghosts and immortals?
The World-Honored One then spoke for him the "Mantra of Immeasurable Majestic Virtue, Sovereign Radiance, and Supreme Wondrous Power."
It is said that if one recites this mantra, it can transform a small amount of food and drink so that all the *piśāca* and *ṛṣi* spirits may each attain full satiety.
Ānanda, by practicing according to these instructions, was able to extend his lifespan, and the spirits attained rebirth in heaven.
This dharma-gate not only benefits the present but is intended to reach far into the future. The Arhats compiled it into written form, and it has been transmitted down through the Tripiṭaka.
The people of this land have received its great bounty to this very day. How magnificent! This is truly an inconceivable Way of broad charity that brings salvation to the masses.
Tonight, a lay follower of pure faith has specially prepared *hūka* offerings for a particular purpose.
Now that the hour of the meal has arrived and the ritual preparations are laid out, we must summon their presence and extend our invitation. (Recite:)
(Thus it is said).
When Ou-yang Wen-t'ung Kung Hsiu once stayed overnight at Ts'ai-shih, he heard the voices of spirits.
While staying at the Ts'ai-shih ferry, Ou-yang Wen-t'ung Kung Hsiu heard voices calling out from the stern of his boat at night, saying: "Go! Come!"
A person who had been summoned replied, "The Senior Minister has stayed here; you must not leave. Please take the provisions for the fast back with you.

Gong silently reflected that the boat’s stern was pressed against the shore and there was no one else about, so it must have been a ghost. At the fifth watch, he again heard the sound of horses galloping rapidly along the bank.
Those at the stern of the boat called out, "What about the provisions for the fast? Those on the bank answered while continuing their pace, "To the ritual site."

Those who were not pure found nothing at all, yet they returned and reported the matter as strange. Half a month later, while traveling to Jinshan Temple, he informed the Elder. The Elder said, "Yesterday, there was a donor at the temple performing a ritual for the second watch of the day. His wife lay nursing her child; after a short while, a foul wind extinguished the candles. At that time, everyone was startled and wondered what it could have been. He replied, "It was this. The Elder said, "How extraordinary! He then had a portrait of him painted and hung it in the hall. Whenever the monks gathered for the midday meal, they would first bow to him. Later, when the donor’s wife became pregnant again, she dreamed of a monk who told her, "I am the one from the previous life. Now I shall be reborn as your son. When the child was born, he was indeed handsome and intelligent. When he grew up, he entered the monastic order and became known as Dharma Master Huichang. He was able to recite the entire *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* from memory. He passed away at the age of seventy-four. It is said that at the time of his death, he sat upright and passed away with a smile on his face. His remains were enshrined in a stupa at Jinshan. It is recorded that whenever incense was offered, a fragrance would permeate the room. This is the reason why the image of the Elder is still worshipped today. Furthermore, in the past, there was a monk named Huishou of Mount Lu, who was diligent in his practice and possessed great supernatural powers. Once, while traveling through the mountains, he encountered a tiger. The tiger crouched before him and licked his feet. Huishou then climbed onto its back and rode it out of the mountain. Regarding the miraculous response to the water and land rites performed by Chan Master Foyin Liaoyuan—whom tradition holds to be an emanation of Rucika Buddha—I did not believe this until later I read...
The fact that Master Miaofeng’s *Poetry Collection* and his stele inscription contain such accounts is indeed as they claim.
It is said that before the Master arrived to visit Chan Master Dajue Liai, one day prior to his arrival, Dajue suddenly dreamed that Louti (Rulai) had arrived.
At dawn, he led the assembly to welcome him, yet the Master had already come. Consequently, Master Liai composed a poem to present to him, addressing him by the name "Louti."
The Master once dreamed that Śākyamuni, his original teacher, told him:
"You are my disciple, the last of the thousand Buddhas of this Bhadrakalpa, the Tathāgata Ruci. Upon awakening from the dream, he composed a verse:
"In the dream, though I spoke as Ruci, Upon waking, I am still but a bhikṣu. I send word to my thousand companions on the Way of Śākyamuni: If you encounter me..."
Regarding the phrase "first extract the head," it is as follows: When the Master was residing at Mount Jin, some sea merchants arrived at the temple to perform a *shuilu* (water-land) ritual.
That night, as the monks were moving along the ritual implements, the Master had no choice but to personally take charge of the *zongchi* (the ritual manual).
That night, a fishing boat was moored at the river rapids; late in the night, he suddenly heard a voice from the bank saying: "Now..."
The night scenery of the golden mountains and waters was most magnificent; this was due to the personal empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Ruci Tathāgata.

The fishermen, having discerned that these were the voices of spirits, conceived a profound sense of reverence and admiration for the Master. From this manifest proof, one knows that when human excellence and the excellence of the Dharma coincide, they move spirits and deities to rejoice and partake of the offerings.

Regarding the miraculous response to reciting the "Verses for Breaking Hell" (*Diyu jietuo ji*), the *Complete Works of Dongpo* states: "If one wishes to fully understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, one should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm:
all things are created solely by the mind. A merchant whose wife had died dreamed that his wife was seeking the "Verses for Breaking Hell"; upon waking, [he recited them].
When they sought it, it was nowhere to be found. Upon questioning the elders of Jianfu Temple, they were told that this verse was indeed it; thereupon, the entire family began to recite it.
Later, they saw the deceased person, clad in precious robes and wearing a celestial crown, floating ethereally in mid-air, expressing gratitude before departing.
Su Shi heard this from Foyin, and Foyin heard it from Fan Yaofu.

The *Huayan Ganying Zhuan* (Biographies of Miraculous Responses Related to Huayan) states: In the third year of the Chuigong era, Dharma Master Fazang of Huayan went to Chongfu Temple and saw Vinaya Master Jian, who said:
"This summer, Shenliang of Guo in Xian'an Ward came to the temple to pay his respects to me.
He told me that he had suddenly died a short while ago and that seven days had passed, yet he has recently been revived. At that time, there were three messengers."
He was pursued to the abode of King Samatā, where the king interrogated him regarding his merits and transgressions.

The king ordered an attendant to lead him to hell, when suddenly he encountered a monk who said, "I shall save you from your suffering; you need only receive and uphold a single verse, and you will surely be liberated from this misery.
The verse said: "If a person wishes to fully understand... Shen Liang recited it in a state of panic for several dozen times before—
Those who share in the same offense shall all be liberated; one should know that this verse is capable of destroying the hells.
Master Zang said that this verse is from the fourth assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Master Jian did not believe him and requested that the nineteenth fascicle be examined; indeed, it was found to be the verse spoken by Bodhisattva Jue-lin.
The *Zuānlíngjì* states: Formerly, there was a man of the Wang family (whose name is lost) from Jīngzhào who died suddenly and returned after three days.

When he departed, he had been pursued by two messengers to the hells. He happened to see a monk who claimed to be from the hells, who immediately ordered him to recite the four-line verse beginning with "If one wishes to fully understand. The King hurriedly chanted it, and wherever his voice reached, [all suffering ceased].
The sinners were all completely released. Once the King had revived, he made a vow to recite it for the rest of his life.

He further recounted this matter to both the clergy and the laity to encourage them to maintain its recitation. At that time, there was a monk who, upon consulting the scriptural texts, discovered that it was a verse from the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
A Record of Miraculous Responses from Reciting the Mantra for Shattering Hell:
Formerly, at Xiaoshi, there was a scholar-official of the Xu clan (whose personal name is lost). The eldest wife of the Xu family fell ill and suddenly passed away.
She then saw a man dressed in the robes of a sovereign, his appearance majestic and imposing. The woman bowed her head to the ground and asked who he was.

The King replied, "I am an official of the underworld. Because every member of your household, great and small, has constantly recited the 'Dharani for Breaking Hell,' all the sinners within the underworld have attained liberation.
You possess such merit that I have come specifically to express my gratitude. The wife was startled and said, "I am but a lowly and humble woman;
how could I be worthy of a sovereign’s supreme gratitude? The King said, "Though you are an ordinary person..."
In days to come, the entire family shall surely be reborn in heaven; therefore, my repayment is such as this.
From now on, you must not forget this mantra.
The mantra is: Oṃ kharadīye svāhā.

Regarding those who now provide food for the deceased, according to the *Madhyama-āgama*, if one makes offerings and sacrifices for a dead person, whether the deceased has entered the realm of hungry ghosts or not, they may receive it in some cases but not in others, because each has their own means of sustenance. This is explained in detail in the *Saṃyukta-āgama*.
Regarding this matter, if one's relatives do not take rebirth within the realms of existence, one need only give with a sincere mind, and they will naturally obtain merit, and so forth.
The *Fozu Tongji* states that there are two reasons for offering "birth-food" (*chusheng fan*): first, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* instructs one to give to those who are destitute...
The *Yegui binailu* (Wild Ghost Vinaya) ordains that offerings be made to the Mother of Ghosts (*Haritī*) and her like;

these beings originally ate flesh and devoured humans, but after the Buddha converted them, they received the precepts against killing. He then instructed his disciples to provide food for them wherever they were.

This refers to the practice where each hall in the monastic complex provides food for sentient beings. These two points are based on the *Yankou jing* (Sūtra of the Mouthful of Food), which was entrusted to Ānanda.
To provide for the hungry ghosts as a condition for their receiving food, one should now separately prepare small measures of grain in the refectory;

after the meal is finished, the assembly performs the ritual of Dharma-giving, or each person prepares a small vessel of raw grain to offer through incantations at night—this is a practice that applies universally to all lineages.

Furthermore, it is said that the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "One should give a single meal to all beings" (the term "all" fully encompasses the six realms), and only after making offerings to all Buddhas and the multitude of worthy sages may one eat.
The *Nanyue Suiziyi Samādhi* says: Whenever one obtains food, one should say:
"May the color, fragrance, and flavor of this food be offered above to the Buddhas of the ten directions, presented in the middle to all the worthy sages, and bestowed below upon..."
In the *Liudao pin* (Chapter on the Six Realms) and other texts, it is taught that giving is without distinction (the character "chu" [chǔ] is pronounced as "chù"; it means not being uneven).

According to the Tiantai method of contemplating the mind through eating (*guānxīn shífa*), after the bell has been struck, one should clasp the hands in worship to offer to the Three Treasures in One Body. Next, one generates the food and recites the names of the six realms to bestow it upon them. These are all equal offerings to the ten dharma-realms;
this is clear evidence for the practice of the current generation in bestowing gifts upon the six realms by performing the Water and Land (*shuǐlù*) rituals. — Narrated.

The *Miaole* says: "As for the worldlings who establish the six realms, this was because Emperor Wu of Liang saw that there were many licentious sacrifices in Jiangdong (where life was taken to sacrifice to heterodox spirits), and thus he used a provisional substitute based on similar Buddhist principles.

This was likely Jingxi’s initial approach of contrasting the evil practice of sacrificial rites with the Buddha-dharma; it was intended to stop the killing throughout the empire, and thus he did not yet discuss the ten realms."
Regarding the meaning of "equal offerings," the *Ullambana Sūtra* (Yan kou jing) instructs that making offerings to the Triple Gem constitutes the offering to the four noble paths;
offerings to Brahmins and seers constitute the offering to the human path; and offerings to the assembly at the *Ullambana* feast constitute the offering to the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).

Although the other four realms are not explicitly detailed, this is likely because the teaching was adapted to the specific capacities of the audience at that time and was not yet universal; thus, the scriptural text is concise and abbreviated. For a practitioner of the Mahāyāna who practices through perfect contemplation...
Regarding the Dharma-realm, one should rely on the meaning found in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
As for Ciyun’s claim that beings in the realm of ghosts obtain food while those in the other five realms do not—this view also draws upon the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, which states:
"If it is due to a sacrificial offering, only ghosts and spirits obtain it; the other destinies cannot fully obtain it. This, however, refers specifically to human-world sacrifices. If...

If one relies on supramundane dharmas and practices unimpeded offerings with a mind of equanimity, then by looking up to the texts of Vimalakīrti, Nanyue, and Tiantai, one will find that the principle is not absent from any of them.

Nowadays, there are those who prepare small measures of grain for scattering, some using a single large *hu*, others up to forty-nine *hu*; all of these are intended as equal offerings to the multitudes of the six realms.
How could one not believe this chapter?

(The preceding sections have been recorded here for reference; furthermore, regarding the secret ritual for the offering of food and recitation, those who wish to practice it must receive it from a master. As for all mantras and divine spells, if one recites them without having received them from a master, one violates the samaya of the Buddhas; therefore, one should be cautious.)

The Śramaṇa school’s practice of offering food is an inconceivable dharma. By reciting mantras for two weeks (fourteen days), it is claimed that one can reach across the various classes of the six realms and four modes of birth;
by concentrating upon the minute of a single vessel, it is claimed that one can transform four *hu* and nine *dou*.
To measure a *dou* with the hunger of a creature with a scorched belly and a giant mouth, and to claim it can bring about the satisfaction of a full belly filled with sweet delicacies—
is this not a most inconceivable method? If such a thing is inconceivable, yet one does not show what is credible for practice,
then faith will become even more difficult to attain.

Master Xia of Siming extensively examined the scriptures and teachings, and he discerned that the single practice of *śrāddha* (feeding the hungry ghosts) provides particularly abundant benefit and salvation.

He feared, however, that many people might not know its origins; although it is clearly manifest in the canonical records, unless these are synthesized into a unified system, they will remain scattered and difficult to investigate.
Therefore, he has compiled this record as a comprehensive manual for the *śrāddha* ritual, tracing it back to its distant sources.

The Buddha’s own mouth personally proclaimed this, and it has been transmitted through the support and assistance of successive masters until its miraculous responses and efficacy are recorded without exception.
One day, [the author] was brought a copy to show him; the Master washed his hands and purified his heart to read it, discovering things never seen before.
He thought, "Regarding what I previously believed, my faith now increases all the more. Yet, as for those who have not yet believed, how can I remain without means to guide them?"

To open the way for profound faith, he then relinquished his family wealth to commission artisans for its publication, so that those who see it now may know its source and basis and increase their diligence;
and that those who have not yet seen it may develop faith and practice with vigor.
It is hoped that from this point on, everyone will delight in giving food, whereby the fires of hunger in the three miserable realms and the eight difficulties [will be extinguished].
Having completely extinguished [all afflictions], they take birth in superior realms through the power of the Buddha’s vows; how could their benefit not be vast indeed?
